chanoch.definition: Enoch, seventh generation from Adam. The Torah records that he walked with Elokim and was taken, without the refrain “and he died” that closes every other life in Bereishis 5. The name shares a root with chinuch, formation.

chinuch.definition: Education, dedication, formation. Not the insertion of information but the shaping of a person until a path becomes inhabitable from within.

metatron.definition: The celestial identity that Heikhalot literature assigns to the transformed Chanoch. A created being holding an exalted office — never a second deity and never an object of prayer.

heikhalot.definition: “Palaces.” A body of early Jewish mystical literature describing ascent through celestial palaces, in which the identification of Chanoch with Metatron is made explicit.

sar-hapanim.definition: Prince of the Presence. A title of position relative to the Divine Presence — a face turned toward the lower orders while remaining a servant before what is above.

naar.definition: Youth, or servant-lad. Applied to Metatron it denotes permanent formability and availability to be sent, rather than immaturity.

sofer.definition: Scribe. One whose entire discipline is fidelity in transmission; a scribe who improves the text has destroyed it.

shem.definition: Name. In this context, the way the Unnameable becomes addressable — a revealed relation, never the Essence itself.

havayah.definition: The customary respectful designation used in Chassidic writing for the four-letter Divine Name, avoiding its pronunciation and its decorative use.

havayah-hakatan.definition: “The Lesser Havayah.” A title from later Kabbalistic reception designating a garment through which governance is mediated to lower orders. Always read here through bittul and the Creator/created distinction.

atzmus.definition: Essence. In Chassidic usage, the Divine as it is in itself, distinguished absolutely from every revelation of it, however exalted.

giluyim.definition: Revelations, disclosures. The counterpart to Atzmus: what is shown, which is never identical with the One who shows it.

levush.definition: Garment. That which makes light bearable to a receiver without being the light's origin. The wearer is not the garment.

bittul.definition: Self-nullification — more precisely, the surrender of the claim to be an independent source. Not the erasure of the self but the emptying of false authorship.

malchus.definition: Kingship; the tenth and final sefirah, the receiving and speaking faculty of the sefirotic order, and the point from which a lower world begins.

leis-lah.definition: “She has nothing of her own.” The Zoharic description of Malchus — and, in this study, the condition that makes total reception possible.

nukva.definition: The receptive aspect within the sefirotic structure. Interiority, containment and hospitality as strength rather than as absence.

mekabel.definition: Receiver. In this study, an active role: the receiver adds form, location and answer to what it is given.

or-yashar.definition: Direct light. Illumination as it descends from source toward receiver.

or-chozer.definition: Returning light. The ascent produced by a receiver who has answered — which completes the circuit that direct light alone leaves open.

keser.definition: Crown. Encircling light that rests above the head without being produced by it — and, crucially, without severing itself from it.

makif.definition: Encircling light: illumination that surrounds a vessel it exceeds, rather than being contained within it.

shechinah.definition: The Divine Presence as it dwells. The word shares a root with dirah, dwelling — indwelling rather than visitation.

dirah-betachtonim.definition: “A dwelling in the lower realms.” The purpose of creation in Chassidic teaching: not that the world ascend, but that the lowest place become a home.

basi-legani.definition: “I have come into My garden.” The maamar associated with the mandate of the seventh generation to draw the Shechinah downward into the lowest world.

dor-hashevii.definition: The seventh generation. In Chabad usage, the generation charged with completing a downward movement rather than achieving a higher ascent.

shemini.definition: Eighth. Used in this study strictly as contemplative symbolism — what completion is for — and never as an institutional proclamation.

middos.definition: The seven emotive attributes of the sefirotic order, completed and made transmissible by Malchus.

tzaddik.definition: A righteous person. Rashi's reading of Chanoch insists that righteousness and vulnerability are not mutually exclusive.

acher.definition: “Other.” The name given to Elisha ben Avuyah after his apostasy. The Talmudic account of his ascent supplies the tradition's own warning against inferring two authorities from Metatron's exaltation.

pardes.definition: The orchard entered by four sages in the Talmudic account of mystical ascent, of whom only one emerged whole.

shtei-rashuyos.definition: “Two authorities.” The dualistic conclusion the tradition treats as the catastrophic misreading of an exalted servant.

tzimtzum.definition: Contraction or self-limitation, making room for a receiver. Writing is a small instance: an intention accepts a shape in order to be transmitted.

tzelem-elokim.definition: The Divine image in the human being. In this study, the ground of the claim that enormous capacity requires deeper surrender rather than less.

veinenu.definition: “And he was no more.” The phrase that replaces the expected refrain of death, read here both as concealment and as the softening of a separate centre.

sinai.definition: The giving of the Torah at Sinai, after which holiness enters matter through mitzvos rather than requiring the holy person to be taken up out of it.

kiddush.definition: The sanctification spoken over wine on Shabbos — the essay's chosen image of Divine will entering grapes, glass, a hand and a table.

tefillah.definition: Prayer. Read in this study as or chozer: speech that answers rather than speech that demands.

avodah.definition: Service, and the inner work of it. The measurements describe the palace; the avodah tells us why the palace matters.

guf.definition: Body. In the essay's argument, not the obstacle to holiness but the destination of it.

keilim.definition: Vessels. The future imagined here is not a world without vessels but a world whose vessels have become transparent to their purpose.

tohu.definition: Chaos; in Kabbalistic usage, a state of great light in vessels unable to contain it. The essay's name for capacity without bittul.

chassidus.definition: The Chassidic teaching, and in particular the Chabad discipline of bringing the highest concepts into a form that transforms the person contemplating them.
